title: HTTP Caching & CDNs

subtopics.title: Freshness
subtopics.explanation: A cache stores a response so it can be reused. The max-age directive gives a response a freshness lifetime in seconds. During that window, a cache can answer without contacting the original server. It is like a printed menu that is valid until its date expires.

subtopics.title: Browser cache
subtopics.explanation: The browser can keep files on a person’s device. Returning visits may load these files locally. Use long lifetimes for versioned files whose URLs change when their contents change. Keep HTML fresh enough to point to the latest assets.

subtopics.title: CDN edge cache
subtopics.explanation: A CDN keeps copies at locations near users. A request can be answered by a nearby edge instead of travelling to the origin server. Public static files are common candidates. It works like stocking popular goods in nearby shops.

subtopics.title: Validation
subtopics.explanation: After a response becomes stale, a cache may ask the server whether it changed. Conditional headers can let the server confirm that the saved copy is still current. A validation response can be smaller than sending the whole file again.

subtopics.title: Personalized data
subtopics.explanation: A response that depends on the signed-in user must not be shared with strangers. Cache keys and privacy rules need care. Use private or no-store directives when appropriate. A shared mailbox must never contain someone else’s private letter.

foundations.overview: Browsers and CDNs reuse responses to reduce repeat downloads and latency.
foundations.whyItMatters: These ideas affect how quickly, reliably, and safely a frontend works.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser and CDN evaluate freshness, validators, cache keys, and privacy directives. DevTools can show whether a response came from memory, disk, or a network edge.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use immutable caching for content-hashed assets. Revalidate HTML and keep account-specific responses private.
foundations.businessImpact: Caching lowers wait time and origin traffic, but stale or shared private responses can damage trust.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Write a cache policy for each response class instead of copying one header everywhere.
foundations.performanceImpact: A cache hit can avoid a network round trip. Confirm hit rates and freshness with real traffic.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A CDN automatically makes every page faster
commonMisconceptions.reality: A CDN helps only when content and cache rules allow a useful edge response.

commonMisconceptions.myth: No-cache means never store the response
commonMisconceptions.reality: It usually means validate before reuse; no-store asks caches not to store it.

keyTakeaways: A cache stores a response so it can be reused.
The browser can keep files on a person’s device.
A CDN keeps copies at locations near users.
